planting.note: Set huli (corm tops) or whole corms once soil has warmed; can be grown in either boggy wetland beds or evenly moist upland rows.

directions: This is the traditional 'ordinary' Hawaiian poi taro, grown successfully in both flooded wetland patches and evenly moist upland beds beneath light tree cover. Its yellowish-green petioles and purplish-lilac corm flesh are the source of prized 'Lehua red poi,' a variety long favored across the islands for home and small-farm cultivation. Give it rich, consistently damp soil and some afternoon shade in hot Gulf Coast summers to keep leaves from scorching, and expect corms ready to dig 8 to 12 months after planting. Corms and the young leaves must be thoroughly cooked to break down calcium oxalate before eating.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii database (Lehua Maoli)

planting.note: Best suited to a permanently flooded or continuously saturated bed rather than ordinary garden soil, mimicking a wetland lo'i.

directions: Historically one of the most important commercial poi taro varieties on Oahu, this stocky, erect selection is grown almost exclusively as a flooded wetland crop rather than in upland beds. It tolerates lowland heat and humidity with less corm rot than many other wetland types, making it a sturdy choice for a pond-edge or bog planter in a partly shaded Gulf Coast garden. Keep the roots submerged or saturated at all times and expect a long season, with corms maturing 12 to 15 months after planting. The chalky-white corm flesh must be cooked before eating.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii database (Piko Uliuli)

planting.note: Grow as an upland taro in evenly moist, rich beds rather than flooded water; underplant beneath open tree canopy for part-day shade.

directions: Grown principally as a table taro rather than for poi, this medium, well-spreading, stocky cultivar is traditionally raised under upland rather than flooded culture. It suits a shaded border bed kept constantly damp rather than a true bog planting, and its white, yellow-fibered corm flesh cooks up firm for boiling or roasting. Expect corms to size up roughly 9 to 12 months after planting corm sections or huli. As with all taro, cook corms and greens thoroughly before eating to break down irritating calcium oxalate crystals.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii database (Niue-ulaula)
